FORMAT MODE
Single continuous seven-second take. No cuts, no transitions, no fades. Real-time motion.

OPTICS
47° diagonal field of view, standard normal lens character, 50mm-equivalent perspective, zero distortion. Camera 0.95 to 1.05 metres from the hand, lens about 50 cm off the floor and almost level, tilted only about 2° down. Lens character locked at 47° for the whole take — no zoom, no field-of-view drift, no lens breathing.
Wide-open aperture behaviour with a thin focus plane on the hand, and that plane is resolved to its physical limit: the back of the hand, the knuckles, the tendon lines and the pores razor-sharp, individual hairs on the forearm separately visible, the ridge pattern on the finger pads readable. This is the sharpest and most detailed area of the frame by a wide margin. The forearm softens above the wrist; the armrest end cap is just off sharpness while its stitched seam still reads; the tunic folds keep their fold structure without weave; the leg and coat of <<<image_2>>> sit outside the focus plane — only thirty centimetres back, so their outline, the knee bulge and the long crease stay clear while the weave is gone, soft but never a shapeless mass. The unlit depth at the right edge is the softest part of frame and its small lights render as clean round bokeh with a gentle bloom. Focus stays on the hand for the whole take apart from one small hand-pulled correction around 4.5s that drifts a few millimetres and lands back on the knuckles.

SURFACE AND TEXTURE
The hand is the most detailed object in the frame and it reads as photographed skin. Across the back of it: skin pores everywhere, each catching its own minute shadow; a network of veins raised under the skin, following the metacarpals and sinking away at the knuckles; four extensor tendons as faint slack lines; the skin over the knuckles gathered into small dry creases that fan out when it stretches; fine hairs, individually resolved, sparse low on the back of the hand and thicker up the forearm. On the fingers: creases banded around each joint, visible ridge patterns on the pads, matte nail plates with a faint lunula, a free edge slightly uneven on one or two nails, and nail beds darkened by pooled blood.
The skin colour is not uniform: a shade redder over the knuckles, a shade more sallow along the tendon lines, deeper and duskier toward the fingertips, and thin enough over the wrist bone to show the bone's shape with a couple of flexion lines across it.
Film grain sits on top of all of it, finest in the sharp plane. The benchmark for detail: if this frame were enlarged, the smallest thing still resolvable on the hand would be a single pore or a single hair — every square centimetre of skin carries texture at that scale, and the same is true of the cracked leatherette of the armrest and the woven cloth of the tunic within their own sharpness.

ACTION TIMING
This shot contains one event and a stillness after it, and the stillness is the point. The timing of the hand follows <<<video_1>>> exactly.
0.0s to 1.2s. The hand hangs in the passive curl described above. Across the back of it the four extensor tendons read as faint slack lines under the skin. Nothing moves but the camera.
1.2s to 1.9s. THE LAST CONVULSION DRAWS THE HAND IN, and it takes its time — about three quarters of a second, not a snap. The fingers curl inward toward a weak closed shape, travelling perhaps a centimetre at the fingertips, closing on nothing and never reaching a hard fist. As they draw in the knuckles rise, the extensor tendons over the back of the hand pull taut, and the skin across them tightens so the dry creases over the knuckles stretch open. The wrist stays slack at its full passive angle and nothing travels above it.
1.9s to 3.0s. THE CURL HOLDS for over a second, and inside that held tension a fine fast quiver runs through the fingers — under a millimetre of travel, irregular, the tremor of muscle with nothing left to hold with. The hand neither closes further nor opens during this second.
3.0s to 4.4s. THE TENSION LETS GO SLOWLY. The quiver stops first, then the fingers open back out under their own weight across about a second and a half — slower than the closing was, damped by the tissue itself, drifting slightly past where they started as the tendons sink back into the skin. No snap, no rebound, nothing catches. The hand comes to rest a millimetre or two more open and marginally lower than it began, because the tone that was holding it is gone.
4.4s to 7.0s. Nothing. For the last two and a half seconds the hand hangs completely lifeless in that final position: no tremor, no twitch, no drift, no swing, not one finger moving, not one tendon shifting. The convulsion happens once and only once, and it is confined to the hand: the wrist never rotates, the forearm never lifts, the arm never shifts its weight on the armrest, and nothing enters frame to touch the hand. After 4.4s no part of the hand moves again for any reason.

PHYSICS
The hand carries real dead weight: the flesh hangs off the bone, the fingers hold the curl gravity gives them rather than a posed shape, the wrist is slack at its full passive angle, and the pads of the fingers are pulled toward the floor by their own mass. The convulsion is an active flexor contraction against gravity — drawn in over three quarters of a second, held and trembling for a second, then released — and the release is passive, so the opening is slower than the closing and damped by the tissue itself, never elastic and never bouncing. Because the flexors are the ones pulling, the mechanics show on the side facing camera: the knuckles rise, the extensor tendons over the back of the hand pull taut and then slacken, and the neighbouring tendons are dragged through their connective bands without any muscle of their own firing. Muscle tone leaves with the release, so the hand's final resting curl is slightly more open and slightly lower than its first — a limb that has stopped holding itself. Venous pooling darkens the fingertips and the nail beds slightly, the lowest part of the hand. The armrest pad is soft leatherette over foam and holds a visible compression dent under the forearm; that dent does not change, because the forearm never shifts its weight. The tunic keeps its folds. The cloth of <<<image_2>>> hangs plumb and stays exactly where it hangs; heavy wool at rest does not stir on its own. The camera's mass shows in every correction: motion begins and ends with weight and never snaps.

LIGHTING
One source lights this entire frame: a single large soft cool white source, above and slightly camera-left, angled about 45° down and nearly on the camera axis horizontally — the overhead tube of the interior. It is out of frame. There is no second source, no light from behind the subjects, no light from the right side, no bounce card and no fill unit: everything not directly lit is lit only by that source's own falloff.
It is soft in its transitions and directional in its rake. Soft means the shadow edges are wide and gradual and there is not one hard shadow edge anywhere in the image, and no shadow crosses the hand. Directional means it still grazes the surface it lands on: every pore, every hair, every crease over a knuckle and every crack in the leatherette carries its own small shadow, so the skin holds high micro-contrast even under this soft light. The softness lives in the shadow transitions, never in the surface of the skin.
What it reaches, brightest first: the upper surface of the forearm and the tops of the knuckles, carrying one broad sheen and no points of light — the skin is matte and every highlight on it is a wide gradient; the lit top faces of the tunic folds on the left, especially the long fold ridge; the lit upper surface of the standing leg and the broad even sheen on its knee; one dim sheen along the stitched top edge of the armrest and another on the pebble-grained leatherette below it. What it does not reach falls away smoothly: the valleys between the folds, the underside of the standing leg, the underside of the curled fingers, and the top of frame above the leg.
THE EXPOSURE LADDER, HELD CONSTANT: skin on the back of the hand sits about a stop and a half above the lit faces of the blue cloth; the brightest patch of sheen on the upper forearm about a stop above the rest of the skin and never clipped; the shaded sides of the folds and the lower leg about two stops under the lit cloth; the fold valleys and the leg's underside about three under; the top of frame above the leg and the far right corner four or more stops down into true black. Nothing in frame is blown out and nothing but those two areas reaches black.

PHYSICS
The hand carries real dead weight throughout: the flesh hangs off the bone, the fingers hold the curl gravity gives them rather than a posed shape, the wrist is slack at its full passive angle, the pads pulled toward the floor by their own mass.
THE CONVULSION in Shot 1 is an active flexor contraction against gravity — drawn in over three quarters of a second, held and trembling for a second, then released — and the release is passive, so the opening is slower than the closing and damped by the tissue itself, never elastic and never bouncing. Because the flexors are the ones pulling, the mechanics show on the side facing camera: the knuckles rise, the extensor tendons pull taut and then slacken, and the neighbouring tendons are dragged through their connective bands without any muscle of their own firing. Muscle tone leaves with the release, so the resting curl afterwards is slightly more open and slightly lower than before.
THE FALL in Shot 2 is a dead limb and the mechanics are the point. THE ARM IS A COMPOUND PENDULUM WITH SLACK JOINTS, NOT A RIGID ROD: the upper arm swings about the shoulder, the forearm lags behind it about the elbow, the hand lags behind the forearm about the wrist, and each segment reaches the bottom of the arc a fraction after the one above it, so the arm visibly whips rather than sweeping as one piece. The fingers, having no tone at all, trail last.
DAMPING COMES ONLY FROM JOINT FRICTION AND SOFT TISSUE, because nothing is ever touched: about forty-five percent of amplitude survives each swing, so it takes five diminishing swings to die instead of two or three. Nothing about the motion is elastic — it never bounces, never springs back and never oscillates cleanly like a weight on a string, and each swing is slightly slower than a rigid pendulum of the same length because the joints absorb and release out of phase.
THE RELEASE IS FRICTION GIVING WAY, NOT AN EVENT: skin and cloth on smooth leatherette let go in small uneven stages, so the creep is jerky and slow before the slide becomes continuous. The wrist folds back at the extremes of the arc under the hand's own inertia. Venous pooling darkens the fingertips and nail beds, more so once the hand hangs lower than the wrist. The armrest pad is soft leatherette over foam: the compression dent stays visible after the arm has gone and eases only very slowly, still readable at the last frame. The tunic keeps its folds and is not disturbed by the fall. The cloth of <<<image_2>>> hangs plumb and does not stir; heavy wool at rest does not move on its own. The camera's mass shows in every correction: motion begins and ends with weight and never snaps.

The hand is the most detailed object in both frames and it reads as photographed skin. Across the back of it: skin pores, each catching its own minute shadow; a network of veins raised under the skin, following the metacarpals and sinking away at the knuckles; four extensor tendons as faint slack lines; small dry creases over the knuckles that fan out when the skin stretches; fine hairs, sparse low on the back of the hand and thicker up the forearm. On the fingers: creases banded around each joint, ridge patterns on the pads, matte nail plates with a faint lunula, a free edge slightly uneven on one or two nails, nail beds darkened by pooled blood.
The skin colour is not uniform: a shade redder over the knuckles, a shade more sallow along the tendon lines, deeper and duskier toward the fingertips, and thin enough over the wrist bone to show the bone's shape.
In Shot 1 that detail resolves to a single pore and a single hair. In Shot 2 it resolves to a knuckle crease and a nail edge. When the arm is moving fast through the middle of a swing the skin carries real motion blur along the direction of travel while its texture still reads at the ends of the arc where it slows. The cracked leatherette of the armrest and the woven cloth of the tunic carry their own texture within their own sharpness. Film grain sits on top of all of it, finest in the sharp plane.

PHYSICS
The hand carries real dead weight throughout: the flesh hangs off the bone, the fingers hold the curl gravity gives them rather than a posed shape, the wrist is slack at its full passive angle, the pads pulled toward the floor by their own mass.
THE CONVULSION in Shot 1 is an active flexor contraction against gravity — drawn in over three quarters of a second, held and trembling for a second, then released — and the release is passive, so the opening is slower than the closing and damped by the tissue itself, never elastic and never bouncing. Because the flexors are the ones pulling, the mechanics show on the side facing camera: the knuckles rise, the extensor tendons pull taut and then slacken, and the neighbouring tendons are dragged through their connective bands without any muscle of their own firing. Muscle tone leaves with the release, so the resting curl afterwards is slightly more open and slightly lower than before.
THE FALL in Shot 2 is a dead limb and the mechanics are the point. THE ARM IS A COMPOUND PENDULUM WITH SLACK JOINTS, NOT A RIGID ROD: the upper arm swings about the shoulder, the forearm lags behind it about the elbow, the hand lags behind the forearm about the wrist, and each segment reaches the bottom of the arc a fraction after the one above it, so the arm visibly whips rather than sweeping as one piece. The fingers, having no tone at all, trail last.
DAMPING COMES ONLY FROM JOINT FRICTION AND SOFT TISSUE, because nothing is ever touched: about forty-five percent of amplitude survives each swing, so it takes five diminishing swings to die instead of two or three. Nothing about the motion is elastic — it never bounces, never springs back and never oscillates cleanly like a weight on a string, and each swing is slightly slower than a rigid pendulum of the same length because the joints absorb and release out of phase.
THE RELEASE IS FRICTION GIVING WAY, NOT AN EVENT: skin and cloth on smooth leatherette let go in small uneven stages, so the creep is jerky and slow before the slide becomes continuous. The wrist folds back at the extremes of the arc under the hand's own inertia. Venous pooling darkens the fingertips and nail beds, more so once the hand hangs lower than the wrist. The armrest pad is soft leatherette over foam: the compression dent stays visible after the arm has gone and eases only very slowly, still readable at the last frame. The tunic keeps its folds and is not disturbed by the fall. Nothing on the console moves, no lamp changes, nothing switches. The camera's mass shows in every correction: motion begins and ends with weight and never snaps.

LIGHTING
One source lights both shots: a single large soft cool white source, above and slightly camera-left, angled about 45° down and nearly on the camera axis horizontally — the overhead tube of the room, out of frame in both. There is no second source, no light from behind the subject, no light from the right side, no bounce and no fill: everything not directly lit is lit only by that source's own falloff. THE CONSOLE'S INDICATOR LAMPS ARE NOT A LIGHT SOURCE — they are tiny, they are out of focus, and they illuminate nothing at all: not the console, not the seat, not the tunic and not the skin.
The source is soft in its transitions and directional in its rake. Soft means the shadow edges are wide and gradual and there is not one hard shadow edge anywhere in either image, and no shadow crosses the hand. Directional means it still grazes the surface it lands on: every pore, every hair, every crease over a knuckle and every crack in the leatherette carries its own small shadow, so the skin holds high micro-contrast even under this soft light. The softness lives in the shadow transitions, never in the surface of the skin.
What it reaches, brightest first: the upper surface of the forearm and the tops of the knuckles, carrying one broad sheen and no points of light — the skin is matte and every highlight on it is a wide gradient; the lit top faces of the tunic folds, especially the long fold ridge; the lit upper surfaces of the console housing and the top edge of its projecting panel; one dim sheen along the stitched top edge of the armrest and another on the pebble-grained leatherette. What it does not reach falls away smoothly: the valleys between the folds, the underside of the console lip, the underside of the curled fingers, the top of frame above the console.

The sky and air stay clear of any floating paper, kite fragments or drifting debris, and the city below stays in the <<<image_2>>> architectural language throughout. For the entire sequence the pair flies at enormous altitude, close to a kilometre above every roof, tower and spire, so the city always reads as a tiny distant carpet with its river far beneath them and never as nearby rooftops at their own level. In Shot 1 the camera stays far higher than the raven and hunter — about 90 meters above — with a severe downward tilt of roughly 50–55°, looking onto their backs and the tops of their wings, never level with them and never below, and it frames them small in the central third with the city held in deep defocus around them. The raven's airspeed stays ferocious in every shot, with the ground streaking past far below, and a strong gusting wind acts on them throughout, shoving the whole flying mass off its line and snapping coat, hair and feathers in hard bursts. The three shots run at approximately 32% / 30% / 38% of the runtime with exactly two hard cuts.

SCENE CONTEXT
Rider's-eye view from the back of a giant black raven flying fast above an old timber-framed town. The raven noses over into a committed dive straight at the small leaded window high in the gable of a half-timbered house. The rider hauls both chain reins to drag the bird off that line; the raven holds the line, fights the reins, and begins to shrug him loose as the window rushes up.

FORMAT MODE
Single continuous take, no cuts. Real-time motion. Rider point of view for the entire shot.

OPTICS
84° diagonal field of view, classic wide-angle lens character, foreground subjects at 0.6 to 1.2 meters from camera. Strong but natural perspective expansion: the raven's nape and the rider's fists loom large while the town stays visible to all four frame edges; timber lines and roof ridges stay rectilinear. Deep depth of field — feather barbs on the nape and slate courses on the distant roof are both readable. The target house stays small and legible for most of the shot and only swells in the last two seconds, the way a real approach looks. Speed reads through parallax: near roof edges tear across frame while the distant town drifts slowly.

CAMERA
Head-mounted rider point of view, locked between the raven's wings, above its spine, behind its skull for the whole shot. Camera height is the rider's eye line, one meter above the raven's back, tilted eight degrees down at the start.
The camera has a body attached to it: the rider's breathing, the shock of every wingbeat coming up through the saddle, a beat of lag on every turn because a head is heavier than an eye. It pitches down with the bird and over-swings as his head is thrown forward, then catches. It rolls four to six degrees against the direction of every rein pull.
Eye line stays locked on the window; when the raven's head swings off axis the camera follows the beak for a beat, then snaps back to the window. Focus holds on the window from first frame to last. All motion in frame is bird-driven and rider-driven, transmitted through the saddle and the rider's neck.

ACTION TIMING
0.0s to 0.8s — Level cruise at twelve meters per second, eighty-six meters out. Two full wingbeats: on the upstroke the wing wrists sweep up into frame at x 5% and x 95%, y 55%, and the view sinks; on the downstroke the wings drop out of frame and the view surges forward and up. Both fists ride loose, chains slack, fingers riding the links, the camera drifting easy — the rider is still enjoying this. Gable holds steady at six percent of frame width, x 63%, y 43%.
0.8s to 1.4s — The raven initiates. It drops its skull, tucks its nape flat, yaws four degrees screen-right onto the gable and rolls its shoulders over into a dive with no warning. Horizon climbs out of the top of frame, pantile roofs swing up from the bottom, the camera pitches down and over-swings before it catches, hair is thrown forward across the top of frame. Both grips snap shut, wrists locking, breath cutting off mid-exhale. Sixty-eight meters out; gable at eight percent of frame width, x 61%, y 50%.
1.4s to 2.6s — The rider fights. Left fist drags its chain back and down toward the hip to x 12%, y 96%, elbow folding, gauntlet leather creasing hard across the knuckles; right fist punches forward and out to x 90%, y 86%, arm extending, coat sleeve snapping tight over the shoulder panel. Chains go from slack curves to rigid straight lines. Forearms shake under sustained load, tendons standing above the gauntlet cuffs. The raven's head is dragged twenty degrees screen-left, beak swinging off target, neck feathers bunching under the harness ring, one eye rolling back toward the rider — and the flight line does not change. Forty-four meters out; gable at thirteen percent of frame width, x 58%, y 54%, the window now a readable dark slot.
2.6s to 3.6s — The raven answers. One violent head shake side to side, chains ripping a few centimeters back through both gauntlets; the hands re-grab higher up the links; the beak snaps forward onto the window and locks. Wings half-tuck into a swept delta, shoulders pulling tight into the bottom corners, dive accelerating to twenty-four meters per second. Slate resolves into individual overlapping tiles, oak braces into split grain, the lead grid of the window becomes countable. Twenty meters out; gable at thirty percent of frame width, x 56%, y 55%. Chimney stack tears past frame left and out at 3.4s.
3.6s to 4.4s — The flare, and the shake-off. Both wings punch wide open and cup the air, the raven's chest pitches up, the whole aircraft decelerates hard. The rider's mass keeps going: the camera is thrown forward and down, then up and right as the bird's shoulders roll under him. The right chain rips clean out of the right gauntlet and whips away out of frame at x 100%, y 70%, links flashing in the sun. The left fist clamps white-knuckle and is dragged forward and low to x 25%, y 98%, its chain snapping bar-taut. Seven meters out; the plaster gable fills eighty percent of frame width and its edges leave the frame sides.
4.4s to 5.0s — White plaster fills everything. The bird bleeds off the last of its speed and drifts the final meters. The remaining fist hauls back against the chest, one short sharp intake of breath, and the camera stops correcting and simply holds on the oncoming glass: black diamond lattice, warped panes throwing a broken slice of blue sky, dark interior behind them, worn oak sill and deep plaster reveal casting a hard shadow edge, the raven's beak tip and nape still at the bottom of frame aimed into it. Final frame at just over two meters out — the lead lattice stands vertical through the center from x 37% to x 62%, running off the top and bottom edges of frame, white plaster and one dark oak brace filling the rest, the glass still whole.

PHYSICS
The raven has mass. Every downbeat drives the body up and forward and the rider's weight lands into the saddle a fraction late; every upstroke lets the body sink and the rider goes light. That two-beat rise and fall runs through the whole frame.
Feathers behave like feathers: nape feathers slick flat in the airstream, throat hackles fluttering at high frequency, quill shafts flexing and springing back, two or three loose black feathers tearing free during the dive and tumbling past the camera on the airflow rather than straight back.
The chains are heavy steel. Slack chain hangs in a real catenary and swings a beat behind the bird; tensioned chain is a rigid line that transmits the jerk instantly to the harness ring and visibly compresses the neck feathers under it. Links rattle and grind, and when the right chain lets go it travels as a whipping wave along its length.
Leather resists: gauntlets crease across the knuckles under load, buckled straps pull tight and wrist edges dig in, the shoulder seam stretches, and the chain drags across the palm leather with friction before it slips.
Air has force: coat hem cracking in the slipstream, hair whipping chaotically across the top and side edges of frame, the bird's whole airframe trembling at speed.
Perspective obeys distance: near roof edges sweep across frame fast, the distant town drifts slowly, and the target grows on an accelerating curve rather than at a constant rate.
The dive is a real aerodynamic event: the bird gains speed as it loses height and the tuck cuts drag, then the wings cup open and it dumps that speed in a hard flare — and it is that deceleration, not a shove, that throws the rider's mass forward and breaks his right-hand grip.
Everything in frame has weight, and every change of state has a visible cause one beat earlier.

The raven is the initiator of every change of direction; the rider only reacts. The bird chooses the window, holds the line under load, and starts the shake-off on its own.
The flight vector stays locked on the window from 0.8s to 5.0s no matter how far the rider drags the bird's head off axis: the head moves, the trajectory holds.
The window is in frame in the first frame and in the last, and it grows continuously across the shot.
The camera stays the rider's eyes for the full shot: between the wings, above the spine, behind the skull.
The target stays a small leaded diamond-pane window in a white plaster gable, and the shot ends with the glass whole and two meters out.
